item.title: Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will hold ‘Christmases Not Forgotten’ for WWII survivors

item.content:encoded:
The Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will host Christmases Not Forgotten, a gathering honoring Guam’s World War II survivors who missed out on celebrating Christmas during the Japanese occupation.

The event is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Dec. 6 at the Zefiro Ballroom at LeoPalace Resort. It will bring together manåmko’ and their families for an afternoon of fellowship, music, dining, and honoring those whose lives were lost and those who survived WWII.

The Christmases Not Forgotten was created by a committee of the Mañenggon Memorial Foundation, including war survivor advisors Julia Villagomez, Rosa “Tan Chai” Duenas and David D.L. Flores. Foundation founders Willy Flores and Rita Franquez organized the gathering after hearing survivors share their experiences during and after the war. Flores said many survivors recalled missing family being together and gatherings of Christmas celebrations between 1941 and 1944.

Flores and Franquez said survivors recalled that during the war, some were able to say nobenas, or the CHamoru rosary, in secret.

“They could not get together openly, and they definitely could not celebrate Christmas,” Flores said. “They talked about how Christmas was taken from them in 1941, then of course 42, 43, and then 44. Even though the island was basically freed in July and August, still there was no time to put together Christmas in 44.”

The gathering will include live entertainment, a special surprise appearance, a visit from Santa Claus, gifts, and a shared meal. The foundation said their goal is to honor and celebrate the manåmko’ of Guam and those who have survived and lost their lives in WWII.

Admission is free for Guam WWII survivors. Individual tickets are $65. Family tables and corporate sponsorship opportunities are also available.

The foundation hopes the gathering will help preserve their stories and ensure future generations understand the experiences and sacrifices of those who lived through the war.

item.content:encoded:
CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds has requested a briefing from the U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, to discuss concerns about illicit financial activity and the potential role of Chinese money laundering networks in the Commonwealth.

In a Nov. 18 letter to FinCEN acting Director Jenna Casanova, King-Hinds said federal investigations and prosecutions over the years have highlighted concerns about money laundering and other financial crimes linked to Chinese capital in the CNMI.

The delegate said more information is needed to understand how such networks operate, whether they remain active in the Northern Marianas and what steps federal and local officials can take to address potential risks.

King-Hinds requested a briefing with FinCEN officials to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by criminal organizations and to explore possible legislative, regulatory and enforcement measures to strengthen prevention efforts.

She said the CNMI's proximity to East Asia, its integration into the U.S. financial system and its economic ties to the region warrant closer examination of financial crime risks.

King-Hinds said protecting legitimate investment and economic activity while preventing illicit financial networks from exploiting local institutions is critical to the Commonwealth's economic and security interests.

item.content:encoded:
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has declared the day after Thanksgiving - Black Friday - a government of Guam holiday, giving government employees an additional day off this week

In an executive order issued Monday, Leon Guerrero designated Nov. 27 as a government holiday. All executive branch departments and agencies will be closed that day, with the exception of essential personnel and operations deemed necessary by agency heads to protect public health, safety and welfare.

The governor said the additional holiday recognizes the work of public servants while allowing families more time to spend together during the holiday season.

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio also encouraged residents to support local businesses over the extended holiday weekend and practice inafa’maolek by looking out for one another on the roads and in their neighborhoods.

Residents are encouraged to plan ahead for any government services they may need before the Friday closure.

item.title: Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them. That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.

That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.

Milton, who was Dak Prescott's backup all last season, threw three touchdowns and ran for another one in a 39-38 win Thursday in his third start for the Eagles, who signed him off the Dallas practice squad on Oct. 16.

"The guy's a rock star. ... True example of being cool, calm, collected, and just keep playing the next play, no matter what the outcome," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, who was then asked about the long TD passes. "We've seen it in practice a couple of times. The oohs and aahs were still there, but not as much. It was just like you know he can get that throw done."

After 50- and 45-yard touchdown passes to Smith, Milton ran 15 yards for a score in the fourth quarter and threw a 24-yard TD to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left before Philadelphia lined up for a 2-point conversion. Milton connected with Smith in the end zone, but a holding call against Mailata wiped out the tying score before another try was broken up at the goal line.

But the Eagles (4-7), who were down 31-10 early in the third quarter, got one more chance after sacking Prescott on fourth-and-1 for a nine-yard loss to their 48 in the final minute. After a couple of short completions to Smith and a pass interference call against Dallas, Jake Elliott kicked a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.

Milton, signed by the Eagles about the same time they were determining that Jalen Hurts' season was over because of diagnosis of blood clots, completed 21 of 31 passes for a career-best 331 yards.

"You never know when your opportunity is going to come. You never know, when, where, how. The only thing you can do is just prepare yourself," Milton said. "That's just the main thing I did. There wasn't a day where I was in a Cowboys facility and I didn't take notes. I didn't let a day go by where I didn't ask a question. So just being prepared for the moment and I mean, it showed up when it needed to. ... Really trying to hold my emotions in up here. Just thankful for the moment."

While he was sacked five times, and the Cowboys defense had him on the run throughout, Milton made several big plays out of the pocket.

On the 50-yard TD late in the first half, Milton rolled to his left and was in front of the Cowboys sideline when he threw back toward the center of the field — the ball was in the air more than 60 yards before Smith caught it at the goal line. Milton then looked toward the Dallas bench and made some seemingly good-natured gestures with a huge smile on his face.

"Can't even remember doing that, but it was just kind of in a moment," he said.

Then late in the third quarter, while rolling to his right toward his sideline, Milton threw deep to an open Smith, who after the catch had to take only a few steps into the end zone to complete the 45-yard score. Smith had 11 catches for 200 yards.

Milton's quick sprint down the sideline on his touchdown run got the Eagles within 38-30 with 9:09 left.

"He played his butt off. He played really good, made some throws that only he can make," coach Nick Sirianni said. "He played an outstanding game, super composed throughout."

After appearing in four games for Dallas last season, Milton lost his backup role to Sam Howell in training camp this year. But Milton stayed with the Cowboys on their practice squad until getting signed by their NFC East rival.

The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row, 19-11 to the New York Giants in Milton's first start Nov. 8. After a bye week, they won 19-16 last Sunday over Pittsburgh, when Milton got them in range for a field goal and a two-score lead with four minutes remaining and then converted a third down in the final minute that allowed them to run out the clock.

Only one of Milton's regular-season appearances for the Cowboys was at AT&T Stadium, in a 34-17 loss to the Los Angeles Chargers last Dec. 21.

His third start Thursday was only his eighth regular-season game in the NFL after appearing in nine preseason games — six for the Cowboys this season and last, along with three for New England in 2024 after the Patriots drafted him in the sixth round that year.

item.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
item.description: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80. His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.
item.content:encoded:
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.

Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."

Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.

Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.

He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.

His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

item.title: How 260 tons of Thanksgiving leftovers inspired an American icon: the TV dinner
item.description: Producer Matt Ozug is here with me in studio. We have a story that is, I gather, about Thanksgiving leftovers and an American icon. Is that right? MATT OZUG, BYLINE: That's right, Scott. I know you love a good yarn. Well, this one has got it all - invention, post war design and actual tons of frozen turkey.
item.content:encoded:
Producer Matt Ozug is here with me in studio. We have a story that is, I gather, about Thanksgiving leftovers and an American icon. Is that right?

MATT OZUG, BYLINE: That's right, Scott. I know you love a good yarn. Well, this one has got it all - invention, post war design and actual tons of frozen turkey.

DETROW: I love frozen turkey the most out of all those things.

OZUG: (Laughter) Well, how about 260 tons of it? That is how much turkey was going back and forth on refrigerated railcars in 1953...

OZUG: ...Because Swanson's frozen foods has grossly overestimated how many birds they could sell for Thanksgiving.

OZUG: Yeah. But one guy, Gerry Thomas - this is how the story goes - he's a company salesman. And he doesn't see soon-to-be-spoiled meat. He sees opportunity. See, Thomas is a military veteran. He remembers mess kit eating. And he's just been on a plane where he's been served a meal on a tray with three compartments - one for meat, one for starch, one for veggies. And in that moment, he puts it all together.

DETROW: Is it - (whispering) is it the TV dinner?

OZUG: Yeah. That is the legend. But I wanted to get to the bottom of what's really behind that? It seems kind of incredible, right?

DETROW: You know, inspiration strikes in extreme ways at times, but it also feels like a really good story that perhaps a salesperson would come up with to sell a product.

OZUG: Right. It's a good yarn, like I said. OK, here's someone who agrees with you that maybe it's a little too tidy.

MEGAN ELIAS: I'm Megan Elias. I'm the Winiarski Curator of Food and Wine History at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

OZUG: And at the Smithsonian, they've got this display across from Julia Child's actual kitchen. They have...

ELIAS: ...A TV dinner tray from Swanson.

OZUG: It's that iconic. It's in the Smithsonian. But, you know, like I said, Elias, she's got her doubts about this origin story. For one, she says Thomas, you know, he's a salesman. He doesn't know the science of how to turn those frozen turkeys into a meal.

OZUG: But you know who does know? Women specifically, because in the 1950s, there is a whole generation of women who have been trained as home economists working in the food industry.

ELIAS: Men usually have the creative jobs - right? - the so-called creative jobs, you know, marketing and advertising. And women were in those test kitchens, wearing lab coats and aprons.

OZUG: Basically, Elias is saying food origin stories in general, they tend to be kind of murky. You know, everyone experiments with their food. Kids play with their food. And the tech existed to make these frozen dinners. So all the elements are there, but the exact origin story - eh.

ELIAS: It's possible that he had the idea, oh, I wish - right? - we could do something with these turkeys. And what about a turkey dinner?

DETROW: Is there anybody out there with a counterpoint? Are there Gerry Thomas defenders out there who say he is the hero of the story?

OZUG: Yeah. I mean, there are people who say, no, there could be some truth to it. Here's Laura Shapiro. She's a culinary historian.

LAURA SHAPIRO: One version of the origin story - which is that the Swanson company is sitting there surrounded by mountains of frozen turkey. What are they going to do with it? - that has some plausibility.

OZUG: Shapiro and Elias agree. There was this tech there waiting to be used because of World War II.

SHAPIRO: After the war, you have all this machinery up and running. But no longer can you, like, cook the hamburgers, put them in a can, process it, send it to a foxhole where somebody's going to happily eat them. No, that's not going to happen anymore.

OZUG: It's not going to happen, but people tried. Even before the TV dinner, there was something called the frigid dinner. Yeah, yum, right?

OZUG: Not only a bad name, but these early attempts didn't taste very good. Swanson, though, when they got rolling on this, they had a few things going for them. They're a huge company, national name recognition, and they had money.

SHAPIRO: Because they're a big national company, they have a ton of money. So they do this huge national advertising campaign. This product shows up everywhere. They themselves name their marketing campaign Operation Smash.

DETROW: I mean, it seems like it was a smash, right? We are talking about it all of these decades later. It's in the Smithsonian. It became - I feel like it became a key part of '50s and '60s culture.

OZUG: Totally. And Shapiro says, you know what they did that was also a smash hit? They had a killer name.

SHAPIRO: I think the name was just meant to project you into that wonderful American future where TV would be in all of our lives.

OZUG: Yeah, and it's a smash hit. They sell their first TV dinner in 1954 - Thanksgiving turkey, cornbread, stuffing, peas and sweet potatoes - for 98 cents.

item.title: The case for data centers
item.description: Most Americans do not like data centers. They made that very clear in the midterm elections, when local communities overwhelmingly approved moratoriums and restrictions on data center construction. Still, Congress is now debating a bill that would make it easier to build them — and that bill passed the Senate last week .
item.content:encoded:
Most Americans do not like data centers.

They made that very clear in the midterm elections, when local communities overwhelmingly approved moratoriums and restrictions on data center construction. Still, Congress is now debating a bill that would make it easier to build them — and that bill passed the Senate last week .

The case against these facilities is well-established. Less common is an ardent voice of support.

Ted Neitzke is one of those rare proponents. He's mayor of the formerly industrial Wisconsin city of Port Washington, north of Milwaukee and adjacent to Lake Michigan.

"Every revolution has brought an evolution, and that's what I think is happening," Neitzke told NPR last month. "We are living in the early 20th century, just remodeled again. We have Zuckerberg. They had J.P. Morgan. We have Elon Musk. They had Rockefeller."

As mayor, Nietzke supports a controversial data center the size of 500 football fields that's being built on former farm land in Port Washington. Opponents of the project believe it will harm the community. But Mayor Neitzke thinks he's figured out a way to reap its benefits and minimize its downsides.

"I don't understand why a community like ours, who grew up in an industrial base, would fight the fact that we would need this back again," he said.

Even after the midterms delivered a decisive rebuke of data center projects, Mayor Neitzke says his city's data center deal could be a national model, one that resolves many of the concerns Americans have about them.

"There is no better square-foot-value industrial development than a data center," he added, "and a lot of people will get very upset when I say that."
